feed.title: Offence, Defence & OSINT — Useful Sites
feed.subtitle: A hand-curated, annotated link directory across ten areas, from software and AI to security, economics and architecture. Every entry states what the resource does and where it parts ways with its neighbours.

entry.title: Awesome Connected Things Security
entry.summary: A list for security research on IoT, embedded, industrial and automotive systems, gathering hardware attacks, wireless protocols (BLE, Zigbee, LoRa, NFC) and firmware resources. Unlike web-focused security lists it centres on physical devices and the radio layer.

entry.title: Awesome Cybersecurity List
entry.summary: A year-by-year archive of cybersecurity blog posts, write-ups and papers, with entries up to 2026. Unlike tool lists the links are technical analyses to read (exploit chains, CVE write-ups); tools sit in a separate file.

entry.title: Awesome Industrial Protocols
entry.summary: A security-oriented resource list on industrial network protocols such as Modbus, S7 and OPC UA, with a page and dataset per protocol. Unlike general security lists it goes down to the OT/ICS protocol level.

entry.title: ICS Security Tools
entry.summary: Tools, protocol notes, sample pcaps, configurations and guides for industrial control system (ICS/SCADA) security. Unlike general security lists it covers only OT/ICS environments, and includes packet captures and protocol material. Last updated 2025.

entry.title: Kicksecure Documentation
entry.summary: The wiki of Kicksecure, a hardened Debian derivative, covering system hardening, kernel and browser settings, Tor and password management step by step. Unlike generic security checklists it shows how each recommendation is applied at operating-system level.

entry.title: Oh SHINT! It's a Blog
entry.summary: A GitBook site gathering OSINT web-resource and tool lists plus blog posts, with a separate page of newly added resources per year. Unlike a single framework page it has many topic-specific sub-lists; last updated in 2024.

entry.title: OSINT Bible
entry.summary: An OSINT guide of 450+ tools, methods and ethics/legal notes across 35 sections, which also publishes a link-audit report. Unlike pure tool lists it adds a four-step research methodology and legal-framework sections.

entry.title: s0cm0nkey's Security Reference Guide
entry.summary: A hand-curated guide to links and resources split by topic for SOC, pentesting, DFIR, threat intelligence and AppSec. Unlike awesome lists that cover a single area, it collects blue-team and red-team material in one gitbook.

entry.title: WiGLE
entry.summary: Map and search interface for volunteer-collected worldwide Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and cell-tower observations. Unlike IP geolocation services, it indexes wireless access points with location data.

entry.title: Awesome CAPTCHA
entry.summary: A list of CAPTCHA types and libraries used to tell humans from bots. Unlike a single CAPTCHA service, it sets the types and open-source libraries side by side.

entry.title: Awesome Crypto Papers
entry.summary: A list of theory-basics papers on cryptography for non-cryptographers. Unlike textbooks, it points straight to the original papers and orders them for the non-specialist reader.

entry.title: Awesome Cybersecurity Blue Team
entry.summary: A list of detection, monitoring and response tools for the defensive (blue team) side. Unlike offensive lists it focuses on protecting systems and catching incidents.

entry.title: Awesome Detection Engineering
entry.summary: Resources for designing and operating the detection rules that catch attacks. Unlike ready tools it leans into the engineering of “how to write good detections”.

entry.title: Awesome DevSecOps
entry.summary: A list of tools and practices embedding security into the CI/CD pipeline. Unlike separate security tests it places the checks inside the development flow.

entry.title: Awesome Honeypots
entry.summary: A list of decoy systems (honeypots) set up to lure attackers. Unlike general defence lists it focuses only on deception and early-warning tools.

entry.title: Awesome IAM
entry.summary: A resource list for user accounts, authentication and authorisation. Unlike a single identity provider’s docs it is vendor-neutral, treating password storage, sessions, MFA, OAuth and permission models at the level of concepts.

entry.title: Awesome Prompt Injection
entry.summary: A list of tools and papers on the “prompt injection” vulnerability specific to language models. Unlike classic security lists it looks only at the new attack surface of AI systems.

entry.title: Atypical OSINT Guide
entry.summary: A guide gathering OSINT techniques the usual tool lists skip — blockchain tracing, metadata, unconventional sources. Against standard OSINT lists it goes to the corners: it covers little-known methods rather than the tools everyone already names.

entry.title: Awesome Annual Security Reports
entry.summary: A list gathering the annual cybersecurity reports of research consultancies and government agencies in one place. Unlike reading a single report it is vendor-neutral: it sets them side by side so you can strip the marketing and compare the trends.

entry.title: Awesome Black Hat Tools
entry.summary: A list of tools officially presented at Black Hat events, and only those. Against general tool lists it has a bar to entry: each was demonstrated live on stage, so these are field-tested, vetted tools rather than random repositories.

entry.title: Awesome Game Security
entry.summary: A resource list specific to game security — anti-cheat, reverse engineering, protection bypasses. Unlike general reverse-engineering lists it centres on games, gathering domain-specific topics like anti-cheat systems and game protections together.

entry.title: Awesome Hacking
entry.summary: A list that collects awesome lists for hackers, pentesters and researchers. Unlike the individual topic lists it is the index above them: one door into dozens of sub-lists from OSINT to malware analysis.

entry.title: Awesome OSINT
entry.summary: A category-by-category list of open-source intelligence tools and resources (people, domains, social media, geolocation). Unlike a single-purpose OSINT tool it is the map: the field’s most-cited starting index for which tool fits which job.

entry.title: Awesome Web Security
entry.summary: A resource list focused on web security, split by attack class (XSS, SSRF, deserialisation). Against general hacking lists it is narrow and deep: it targets the web layer alone, gathering articles, tools and labs together for each vulnerability type.

entry.title: HackTricks
entry.summary: A knowledge base giving pentest, red-team, web, cloud and privilege-escalation techniques as step-by-step commands. Unlike conceptual security books it is directly runnable: every page is concrete enough to say “throw this command at that port, look for this in the output” — a field reference, not theory.

entry.title: Infosec Reference
entry.summary: A vast security reference under one roof — red team, blue team, DFIR, AppSec and more. Unlike single-topic awesome lists it is holistic: instead of hunting a separate list per specialism, one annotated, organised reference in a single place.

entry.title: MISP Warning Lists
entry.summary: Ready-made lists for weeding false positives out of threat indicators — public DNS resolvers, known cloud ranges, public services. Unlike raw indicator feeds it is the noise filter: it marks the legitimate infrastructure that should not raise an alarm.

entry.title: Not The Hidden Wiki
entry.summary: An open wiki gathering 5,000+ cybersecurity links sorted by specialism. Against the dark-web directories its name plays on, it is entirely clearnet and legitimate: a plain starting point for tools, publications and training recordings, not a hidden service.

entry.title: Offensive-Resources
entry.summary: A resource set covering every branch of offensive security — infrastructure, wireless, IoT, exploit development, cloud — together with labs. Unlike single-topic lists it is broad and lab-focused: it points to environments where you can practise, not just read.

entry.title: OSINT for Countries
entry.summary: A list that sorts OSINT resources by 193 countries and territories. Unlike global OSINT lists it is geographic: if you need a specific country’s public records, registries and local tools, you go straight to that heading.

entry.title: PoC-in-GitHub
entry.summary: A list that automatically harvests CVE proof-of-concept repositories from GitHub and updates daily. Against Trickest CVE it scans GitHub alone: for each vulnerability it states “this repo was published on this date” — a quick route to a PoC (its README warns of malware).

entry.title: Snoop
entry.summary: A username hunter that searches one handle across hundreds of sites. Unlike tools such as Sherlock it weights the CIS/Russian-language web: it covers the regional platforms that western-focused tools miss.

entry.title: ThreatIntel-Reports
entry.summary: A repository that makes the content extracted from thousands of threat-intelligence reports searchable. Unlike the reports themselves it searches inside them: you enter a tool or APT-group name and it lists every report that mentions it at once.

entry.title: Trickest CVE
entry.summary: A repository that automatically gathers and keeps current every known CVE, with links to proof-of-concept code where it exists. Unlike official databases like the NVD it is exploit-focused: if you want to know where a vulnerability’s working code lives, it points straight to it.

entry.title: TweetFeed
entry.summary: A live IOC feed that collects malicious URLs, domains, IPs and hashes shared by the infosec community on Twitter/X, served as CSV/JSON/RSS/API. Unlike commercial threat feeds its source is open social posts and it is free: it turns researcher observations into real-time, machine-readable data.

entry.title: Dark Vortex
entry.summary: Advanced courses on malware development and offensive tooling. Unlike penetration testing training it goes down to evasion and implant development — aimed at red team tool developers rather than at anyone collecting certificates.

entry.title: ISECOM
entry.summary: The non-profit publishing the OSSTMM security testing methodology. Unlike the certification bodies its actual product is the method: a free, vendor-neutral standard describing how testing should be done.

entry.title: Limes Security
entry.summary: An Austrian firm focused on industrial control systems and critical infrastructure, with OT security training. Against general security training it addresses the operational technology side — PLCs and SCADA.

entry.title: Awesome Fuzzing
entry.summary: A compilation of fuzzing resources: tools, books, talks, papers and practice environments. Against the OWASP page the difference is breadth — this is where you go after you understand the method.

entry.title: Cryptologie
entry.summary: Cryptographer David Wong’s blog and notes on applied cryptography. Against academic papers it explains protocols from an implementer’s seat — not the theorem, but where real systems get it wrong.
